segments.speaker: Kur Peter Thon Aduot · SG, UNDP African Youth Co-creators Council (South Sudan)
segments.text: Isn't it? And we have used something that young people really always fall in love with. Letters, poems, songs. And young people are so passionate about these kind of things.

segments.speaker: Kur Peter Thon Aduot · SG, UNDP African Youth Co-creators Council (South Sudan)
segments.text: And I know we do not wait as young people for treaties to bring peace for us. We are inviting young people to create peace by themselves in their own words, in their own languages, one story at a time. So how do we do it? Right.

segments.speaker: Kur Peter Thon Aduot · SG, UNDP African Youth Co-creators Council (South Sudan)
segments.text: We invite young people to write letters. The letters of hope for people they never met. Because there's someone from other tribes that I've never met, and they've been saying that this tribe is bad, this tribe is like this.

segments.speaker: Kur Peter Thon Aduot · SG, UNDP African Youth Co-creators Council (South Sudan)
segments.text: And create. Young people like to create songs, musics, turn painful stories into something that can be shared with other people without fear. Listen.

segments.speaker: Kur Peter Thon Aduot · SG, UNDP African Youth Co-creators Council (South Sudan)
segments.text: We bring young people into the room where they could be able to talk to each other with elders. The other one listens, the other one speaks, and the other one hears. Truly.

segments.speaker: Kur Peter Thon Aduot · SG, UNDP African Youth Co-creators Council (South Sudan)
segments.text: Have you seen now, we have not used any weapons in it, in these three methods. We have not used any lectures. It's just stories and the courage to listen to one another truly.

segments.speaker: Kur Peter Thon Aduot · SG, UNDP African Youth Co-creators Council (South Sudan)
segments.text: And why across generations? We know elders carry the memory from what war caused us. And the future we shall, young people, carry the future that will be shaped by this kind of memories. So when they only talk about each other, when I talk about you, your generation is so bad and all that, you always get some, I think, blame.

segments.speaker: Kur Peter Thon Aduot · SG, UNDP African Youth Co-creators Council (South Sudan)
segments.text: They are not good and all that. But when we allow them to talk to each other, they get an understanding that this is where we got wrong, and this is where we went wrong. So memory without the future, turns into bitterness.

segments.speaker: Kur Peter Thon Aduot · SG, UNDP African Youth Co-creators Council (South Sudan)
segments.text: And future without memory repeats the past. And that's something that I would love us to all those two, the memory and the past should be in the same room. So what I want to invite all of us is that to the young people especially, take one moment today, write a letter, invite another person from different generation and listen to them, so that they can share with you why they did what they did.

segments.speaker: Kur Peter Thon Aduot · SG, UNDP African Youth Co-creators Council (South Sudan)
segments.text: To the institutions, UNDP and other organizations, I'm inviting you, especially the government, make sure youth peace initiatives should sit at the center of regional and national peace building frameworks. And yes, of course, I serve as the Secretary General for UNDP, African Youth Co-Creators Council. These are the critical ideas that we need to listen to and bring on board before decisions are made by UNDP.

segments.speaker: Kur Peter Thon Aduot · SG, UNDP African Youth Co-creators Council (South Sudan)
segments.text: And that's the reason why I would love you to pick one thing. Today, I pick peace as the key thing that I would love to pass to the next generation. So I'm asking you, what are you passing on to the next generation that your children, your grandchildren will be proud of? I'm Korpida Thon from South Sudan, and thank you.

segments.speaker: Aminata Badjie · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you, Peter. Thank you. That was wonderful.

segments.speaker: Aminata Badjie · Moderator
segments.text: I don't know about you guys, but I always enjoy listening to Peter talk. He can go on and on and you'll eventually lose track of time. But thank you very much, Peter.

segments.text: So, our next speaker is from South Africa. She's a South African digital development and communication professional specializing in digital governance, right? Thank you. Digital public infrastructure and emerging technologies.

segments.speaker: Aminata Badjie · Moderator
segments.text: She's also the country consultant for the ITU JIGA initiative, and she'll be taking us through the topic, sorry, Rails for Creativity, How Digital Public Infrastructure Can Unlock Africa's Creative Economy. Ladies and gentlemen, please welcome Andi Sandoval. Thank you.
One, two. Okay. We're ready to go.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. I would like to stand on all the protocols that have been observed here. My name is Andi Sandoval, and I come from South Africa.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: I come from Ngung'o location in Bizana. It's a small rural town in the eastern Cape of South Africa. We only got electricity in our home in 2010.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: Yes, in 2010. Before then, our evenings were spent listening to stories. I still vividly remember my grandmother's stories.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: I looked forward to those evenings. Even when I was away at Rhodes University during my journalism and politics undergraduate studies, those were the evenings I missed most. She had a way of holding our attention, making us imagine people and places we had never encountered.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: Sometimes I wonder what possibilities her storytelling might have found in today's digital world. And then there were Nollywood movies. I remember how Nigerian films made their way into our communities through DVDs.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: There was one called Beyonce and Rihanna. You know that, right? That film had us on a chalk hold in my community. Long before we had streaming platforms, we were watching and sharing stories across the continent.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: Those evenings shaped my path. They led me to more than a decade in television production and radio production, working with stories and people who tell them. Today, I work in digital governance on the systems that decide whose stories get to travel, who gets to participate, and who benefits.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: Looking back, I realize that creativity and cultural exchange were never absent from our communities. What has changed is that infrastructure through which the stories can travel, find audiences, and generate economic value. And that brings me to one question, a big one.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: The internet gave us the power to create and share, but what do we need to own what we make, trade it, and keep its value? Because being able to reach an audience is not the same as building a sustainable business. Being visible online does not necessarily mean being paid fairly, and participating in a global market does not automatically mean having the power to shape the terms in which to participate. This is where digital public infrastructure becomes important.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: Think of it as shared digital foundations that different services, businesses, institutions can build upon digital identity, payments, as well as secure exchange of data, as just some of the examples. Why does this matter to someone who is working in the creative economy? Imagine a designer in South Africa who gets an opportunity to work with a client in another African country. To make it work, she may need to prove her identity or business credentials, share verified information, agree on a contract, and receive payment.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: If every system operates in isolation, she has to navigate that fragmentation herself. President Kagame made a point on Wednesday that speaks directly to this challenge, and I quote him, siloed systems are holding us back. We are not built for isolation, but for collaboration.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: That is one reason shared digital infrastructure matters. It can help different institutions and services work together, making it easier for people and businesses to connect and transect across borders. This is the thinking behind UNDP Africa's Accelerator for Digital Public Infrastructure.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: While its current work is not specifically focused on the creative economy only, it raises an important question. What could these shared foundations make possible for African creatives? We can already see efforts in this direction. The East African community is working towards an interoperable cross-border payment system.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: Rwanda and Tanzania, for example, are developing a bilateral payment system link. Their ambition is to make regional transactions faster and more affordable. Imagine what that could mean for a designer selling work across borders.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: But making it easier to exchange value must also mean protecting the people who are exchanging that value. Easier payments must not mean easier access to our personal information. This is very personal to me.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: Easier payments must not mean easier access to our personal information. A designer should know what information is collected, why it is needed, and who uses it when they make a transaction. Because infrastructure is never neutral.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: A digital identity system can make it easier to access services, but it can also exclude someone who cannot meet its requirements. Data exchange can also improve coordination, but without proper safeguards, it can expose people to harm. So as we build, we must ask, who gets access? Who needs to shape the design of these systems? Who controls the data? And what happens when systems get it wrong? Creatives, particularly women, young people, informal workers, and people with disabilities must have a voice in these decisions.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: Privacy, accessibility, security, accountability cannot be afterthoughts that we apply as tick-boxing exercises at the end of the process. I began by talking about my grandmother because I want us to remember that creativity does not begin with technology. It begins with people.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: And digital public infrastructure is not simply about technology. It is also about governance. The decisions we make about how these systems are designed, who they serve, who is accountable.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: The infrastructure we build today won't just decide how Africa joins the creative economy that already exists. It will also shape what creative economies we get to build for ourselves tomorrow. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Andisa Ndlovu · Country Consultant, ITU
segments.text: Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Aminata Badjie · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you, Andisa. That was indeed very amazing.

segments.text: I am Gift Godfrey Moju from South Sudan. Just like I said, a fashion entrepreneur and a fashion designer. I am the founder and the creative director of a brand called Shem Africa.

segments.speaker: Gift Godfrey Khamis Moju · CEO, Shem Africa
segments.text: Shem Africa is a sustainable fashion brand where we use discarded textile waste and turn them into sustainable fashion products. And when Elizabeth was talking, I was taken back to some years ago when I was at campus. I remember I was studying, I was doing a degree in library and information science, a program that I had never known my whole life, but because the systems or the families that were raised up from believe that there are specific programs in the university that were supposed to attain, they had to push me there.

segments.speaker: Gift Godfrey Khamis Moju · CEO, Shem Africa
segments.text: In my second year at campus, I was in Uganda Christian University. Sadly or fortunately, I decided to withdraw from campus and then I went to start pursuing a course on fashion and design. And a lot of people felt like I made the biggest mistake of my life.

segments.speaker: Gift Godfrey Khamis Moju · CEO, Shem Africa
segments.text: A lot of people thought I was under the influence of drugs because why would you leave a degree that you're doing to pursue fashion and design? They say they call it tailoring. And when we were growing up, they said this is a women's job. And I'm so happy that through persistence and resilience, it has put me here today.

segments.speaker: Gift Godfrey Khamis Moju · CEO, Shem Africa
segments.text: And I believe if I had not made that decision years ago, I would not be standing here. And I want us to take just a second to think about this. What if the clothes that we throw away could become the threads that can weave the future of Africa? So we've got to learn that a lot of us, once we are done or we don't want to use the clothes that we have anymore, we dump them.

segments.speaker: Gift Godfrey Khamis Moju · CEO, Shem Africa
segments.text: And forgetting what happens before these pieces that we wear are produced. Most of the fabrics that we wear are produced or treated with dangerous chemicals that once dumped in the environment, they take too long to decompose and others do not even decompose or they degrade the environment. So as Shame Africa, we thought of using this discarded waste material, turning them into sustainable fashion products.

segments.speaker: Gift Godfrey Khamis Moju · CEO, Shem Africa
segments.text: I'm happy that I'm wearing one of our products, the jacket. And I want to appreciate each and every one that is here and each and every one that came to the marketplace because we have been producing products and testing the market. And I can say a lot of people are appreciating sustainable fashion.

segments.speaker: Gift Godfrey Khamis Moju · CEO, Shem Africa
segments.text: And most of the products that we even came with, people are excited to have them. So why sustainable fashion? One, I already hinted about environmental protection because once we venture into that, we are going to reduce the waste that goes. And a country that I come from, we still are developing and we have one of, I think, the struggling waste management systems.

segments.speaker: Gift Godfrey Khamis Moju · CEO, Shem Africa
segments.text: And we felt like this could be one of our contributions to that. And the other thing is cultural preservation. In all our collections, we make sure that we should at least put a touch of Africa.

segments.speaker: Gift Godfrey Khamis Moju · CEO, Shem Africa
segments.text: And most of the people want to hear about the Ankara fabric or the Kitenge fabric, someone made a call, we attach it to African culture. So now, what do I want us to take away today? If we invest in fashion, or sustainable fashion, we can change the future. How can we do this? Once we have this, we have a lot of ready materials that are available.

segments.speaker: Gift Godfrey Khamis Moju · CEO, Shem Africa
segments.text: And then we can empower the young people through training programs. And I'm so happy that UNDP has programs like that. And some of the people that are partaking of the program in my country, South Sudan, had an attachment at our workshop to do their internship.

segments.speaker: Gift Godfrey Khamis Moju · CEO, Shem Africa
segments.text: So I believe if we can invest in this, we can imagine an Africa that we would love. Thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Aminata Badjie · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you, Gift.

segments.speaker: Aminata Badjie · Moderator
segments.text: And I agree with you. Sustainable fashion is the way to go. And if I ever eventually come to South Sudan, I'm hitting you up because I love your fit.

segments.speaker: Aminata Badjie · Moderator
segments.text: I love the baggy pants. I love the top very much. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Oudy Keita · Designer, artist and peacebuilder (Mali)
segments.text: I am because you are because you are I am. My existence is permitted thanks to others, partly thanks to others, by their actions, by their way of acting and of building together. It is the definition of Ubuntu, the fact of being able to exist because we do things together.

segments.speaker: Oudy Keita · Designer, artist and peacebuilder (Mali)
segments.text: I am Udi Keita. Je suis née et j'ai grandi en France, dans une famille malienne. Dans cette famille malienne, j'ai reçu une double culture, j'ai reçu une double éducation, issue de ma double culture.

segments.speaker: Oudy Keita · Designer, artist and peacebuilder (Mali)
segments.text: Des valeurs m'ont été transmises, la culture m'a été transmise, des saveurs m'ont été transmises, une manière de voir le monde m'a été transmise. J'ai fait une école de commerce, Grenoble Economy and Management et en parallèle, j'ai eu des expériences dans le secteur du luxe. LVMH Fragrance Brand, Kenzo, Givenchy, Parfum Christian Dior, Thierry Mugler Parfum.

segments.speaker: Oudy Keita · Designer, artist and peacebuilder (Mali)
segments.text: J'ai travaillé dans le marketing opérationnel et le marketing développement. Mais malgré tout cela, le 1er novembre 2018, j'ai décidé de poser mes bagages à Bamako, au Mali, le pays de mes parents. De cette culture que j'ai eue, qui m'a été transmise de par mes pères, mes parents, je suis venu au Mali et j'ai eu cette confrontation culturelle.

segments.speaker: Oudy Keita · Designer, artist and peacebuilder (Mali)
segments.text: Tout ce qu'on m'avait appris, tout ce que j'avais vu auparavant, était différent de ce que j'avais découvert dans le pays. Mais cependant, je m'en suis servi pour créer et réaliser une marque de vêtements dans un premier temps, UDK, une marque de vêtements made in Mali, dont je porte justement mes vêtements. Également, par la suite, j'ai créé un établissement nommé Udikaso, qui est un lieu de vie à Bamako.

segments.speaker: Oudy Keita · Designer, artist and peacebuilder (Mali)
segments.text: La question est de savoir de par les réalisations et la transmission, l'héritage reçu par mes pères, qui m'ont permis de me réaliser et d'être la personne que je suis, comment moi, à mon tour, je peux contribuer et redistribuer par mes réalisations pour que d'autres personnes, par la suite, puissent se réaliser à leur tour. Donc, avec UDK, dans un premier temps, avec l'héritage culturel, je fais en sorte de contribuer à l'économie du pays. En tant que designer, il y a une idée qui naît dans mon esprit.

segments.speaker: Oudy Keita · Designer, artist and peacebuilder (Mali)
segments.text: Mais pour conceptualiser, matérialiser cette idée, il me faut l'aide de toute autre personne. C'est une chaîne qui se met en place. On parle d'intelligence collective.

segments.speaker: Oudy Keita · Designer, artist and peacebuilder (Mali)
segments.text: Un fil, qui permet aux tisserands de tisser le tissu. Ce même tissu va être repris par le teinturier pour être mis dans la teinture. Par la suite, le couturier va prendre ce tissu pour tisser un vêtement.

segments.speaker: Oudy Keita · Designer, artist and peacebuilder (Mali)
segments.text: Puis, finalement, le mannequin porte ce vêtement et le photographe va pouvoir shooter ce vêtement pour que la beauté de ce même vêtement puisse être révélée au monde entier. Vous voyez que nous sommes tous interconnectés, nous sommes tous liés. Je suis parce que tu es, de par tes actions, de parce que nous transformons ensemble.

segments.speaker: Oudy Keita · Designer, artist and peacebuilder (Mali)
segments.text: Nous sommes en mesure de créer et de contribuer à l'économie d'un pays. Lorsque, finalement, ce vêtement rencontre le client final, celui-ci va l'acheter et va communiquer dessus de sorte à ce que d'autres personnes puissent contribuer à leur tour à cette économie. Les vêtements, ce ne sont pas simplement que des vêtements.

segments.speaker: Oudy Keita · Designer, artist and peacebuilder (Mali)
segments.text: C'est un message, c'est un dialogue. Dans le cadre de ma casquette de fashion designer, j'ai été amenée à collaborer avec un artiste nommé Omar Tapili. C'est un artiste qui travaille avec la technique du batik.

segments.speaker: Oudy Keita · Designer, artist and peacebuilder (Mali)
segments.text: Le batik, c'est une technique venant d'Indonésie, mais c'est arrivé jusqu'au Mali. Comme quoi, finalement, nos cultures communiquent. C'est un artiste qui a tendance à faire des tableaux, mais par notre collaboration, je lui ai offert une nouvelle scène de pouvoir s'exprimer à travers les vêtements.

segments.speaker: Oudy Keita · Designer, artist and peacebuilder (Mali)
segments.text: Et de cette création, nous avons pu toucher un nouveau public. Je suis parce que tu es, de par tes actions, de parce que nous construisons ensemble. Être fashion designer, ce n'est pas seulement porter une initiative seule.

segments.speaker: Oudy Keita · Designer, artist and peacebuilder (Mali)
segments.text: Comme ma camarade l'a dit, nous sommes des fondateurs. We are the builder. La dernière action que j'ai eue à mettre en place, c'est Udicasso.

segments.speaker: Oudy Keita · Designer, artist and peacebuilder (Mali)
segments.text: C'est un lieu de rencontre à Bamako où les gens dialoguent, se transforment et se développent. L'un des concepts phares que je n'ai pas inventé, c'est le dîner des inconnus. Lors d'un dîner, des personnes viennent se rencontrer autour d'une table, viennent manger, échanger et apprendre à se connaître.

segments.speaker: Oudy Keita · Designer, artist and peacebuilder (Mali)
segments.text: Pendant ce dîner, il n'y a pas de jugement parce que personne ne se connaît. On peut se réinventer à travers ce que nous souhaitons dégager et communiquer. Lors de ce dîner, il y a deux semaines, j'ai eu le témoignage d'un participant qui, à la fin de la session, a levé la main et m'a dit « J'étais dans un état dépressif, mais grâce à ce dîner, j'ai retrouvé le sourire, parce que justement, j'ai dialogué avec des personnes que je ne connaissais pas, et le fait de pouvoir être écouté, apprécié, a redonné un sens à ma vie.

segments.speaker: Oudy Keita · Designer, artist and peacebuilder (Mali)
segments.text: » Avec Udi Casso, actuellement, on a pu, en tout cas dont j'ai connaissance, il y a eu quatre mariages, deux naissances, des centaines d'amitiés, des entreprises créées et des emplois qui ont pu être rendus possibles par la connexion des gens qui se sont rencontrés. Donc, j'ai décidé de quitter la France pour le Mali. C'est un choix que j'ai fait, mais au vu de mes réalisations et de ce que ça a impliqué, je vois que parce que je suis, j'ai permis à d'autres personnes d'exister et d'impacter leur environnement par les êtres que ces personnes sont.

segments.speaker: Oudy Keita · Designer, artist and peacebuilder (Mali)
segments.text: Je vous remercie.

segments.speaker: Aminata Badjie · Moderator
segments.text: Merci beaucoup, merci beaucoup Udi. Et merci aussi de nous avoir montré que avec nos ressources, on peut créer des opportunités pour beaucoup d'autres gens dans le continent.

segments.text: Good afternoon.

segments.speaker: Joshua Bisureka · Finalist, UNDP Rwanda
segments.text: I'm Joshua Bissarruca. They called me Joshua, but I'm not alone. Here I have a big team.

segments.speaker: Joshua Bisureka · Finalist, UNDP Rwanda
segments.text: Actually, we are urban sketchers, as you see on the screen. Just to make the live drawing. But before I start my presentation, let me ask you a question.

segments.speaker: Joshua Bisureka · Finalist, UNDP Rwanda
segments.text: Who has a smartphone here? Anyone who has a smartphone? Everyone has a smartphone or there's no one who has a smartphone? Everyone has. Who knows how technology or smartphones disconnect us from our identity? Anyone who figured it out? Or is it me alone? Anyone know? Okay. I see you are busy.

segments.speaker: Joshua Bisureka · Finalist, UNDP Rwanda
segments.text: In Kinyarwanda, we say, Avishi ze hamungi, hachi wana nila. It means that the unity makes strength. You know, as most of the time, the artists, they like to be alone in the studio for the creation.

segments.speaker: Joshua Bisureka · Finalist, UNDP Rwanda
segments.text: But for us, as urban sketchers, we have a system where we left our studio behind then we come together face to face to make the sketch. You can ask why sketch? The sketch is a backbone of all art this spring. The artists here, they can understand what is it.

segments.speaker: Joshua Bisureka · Finalist, UNDP Rwanda
segments.text: Then during the sketch session, we collect together. We help each other because everyone here in our team, they have the unique talent. The way he or she expresses their feelings or ideas.

segments.speaker: Joshua Bisureka · Finalist, UNDP Rwanda
segments.text: That is why you see here the paintings. We have the fashionists. We have the sculptors.

segments.speaker: Joshua Bisureka · Finalist, UNDP Rwanda
segments.text: In each this spring, we have the members. But all of us, we meet together on the sketch because the sketch is the beginning of all these springs. Then the impact we have in our society where we preserve the culture, especially the iconic place.

segments.speaker: Joshua Bisureka · Finalist, UNDP Rwanda
segments.text: We visit the place, we sketch, we consume, we pay. Then at final, we made this. We made the magazines where we publish our stories including the image we did from the location.

segments.speaker: Joshua Bisureka · Finalist, UNDP Rwanda
segments.text: Furthermore, we made the intercultural collaboration, the books that talk about the culture between the different cultures. For example, here we have the Rwandan image but for the next page, we have another society culture. segments.speaker: Pempo · African Union
segments.text: My central takeaway is young creatives should help shape Africa's peace development policies with the resources and decisions making power to put the ideas in perspective. Let me draw out four key messages from today's program. First, creative livelihoods deserve serious commitment.

segments.speaker: Pempo · African Union
segments.text: Elizabeth's focus on careers and women's empowerment alongside GIF's work on sustainable fashion connects creativity with livelihoods, cultural heritage, and community well-being. Our response should be including fair pay, business support, market access, and protection of creators' work. Second, creative practice deserves a place in peacebuilding.

segments.speaker: Pempo · African Union
segments.text: Cool Peter's focus on poetry, music, and international dialogue puts a practical question before us. How can young people challenge inherited prejudice and build relationships across divided communities? Youth-led creative initiatives should help shape that response. Third, digital access belongs in the creative economy discussion.

segments.speaker: Pempo · African Union
segments.text: Andisa's focus on digital public infrastructure invites us to connect creative skills with affordable connectivity, accessible tools, digital payments, and fair access to audiences. Young creators should help shape decisions on AI, consent, and the use of their work. Fourth, culture and participation belong together.

segments.speaker: Pempo · African Union
segments.text: Odi's focus on cultural resources and social bonds, and Joshua's focus on community art and heritage point towards a practical approach. Involve communities in creating, interpreting, and sharing their own stories. The participatory mural gives us a concrete way to practice that, and I encourage us.

segments.speaker: Pempo · African Union
segments.text: Of course, I won't be partaking in that due to my inability to create. What should these messages mean for us as the African Union? As we mark 20 years of this very, very groundbreaking instrument, which is the African Youth Charter, the proposed protocol offers us a very, very practical opportunity to help strengthen how youth rights translate into everyday opportunities. My recommendation is that young people and young creatives specifically should help shape its development through the relevant consultations and policy processes that are taking place.

segments.speaker: Pempo · African Union
segments.text: The charter already gives us a foundation. Article 11, which again I said yesterday is my favorite, addresses participation. Article 17 addresses peace and security, and Article 20 and 22 address culture and participation in artistic and cultural life.

segments.speaker: Pempo · African Union
segments.text: The task is to make those practical for today's young creators. I would put forward three priorities for consideration in the protocol process. One, meaningful representation by including young creatives in policy consultations, digital rights, safe participation, youth-presented structures, as well as decisions on cultural and peace-building programs.

segments.speaker: Pempo · African Union
segments.text: Two, protection and opportunity. Address fair remuneration, intellectual property, digital rights, safe participation, as well as access to finance, giving particular attention to young women, young people with disabilities, as well as rural youth and those affected by displacement. Three, accountability.

segments.speaker: Pempo · African Union
segments.text: Let us connect commitments to responsible institutions, budgets, timelines, as well as public reporting with young people involved in reviewing the delivery. The Continental Framework on Youth Peace and Security provides us five priority areas. Here is how I propose this would connect them to creative practice.

segments.speaker: Pempo · African Union
segments.text: Participation by including young creatives in peace dialogues and designing national YPS action plans. Prevention by supporting locally designed storytelling, as well as community arts and intergenerational dialogue that addresses prejudice and encourages peaceful engagement. Protection, safeguarding young creatives from threats, harassment and exploitation, with particular attention to young women and those working in conflict-affected areas.

segments.speaker: Pempo · African Union
segments.text: Partnerships and coordination. Connecting youth, culture, education, and peace institutions with creative networks across Africa, as well as local authorities. Disengagement and reintegration.

segments.speaker: Pempo · African Union
segments.text: Where appropriate, let us support voluntary creative learning and livelihoods alongside specialist psychosocial and reintegration services. Across all these five areas, young people should help define the priorities, manage delivery, and assess the results. To take this forward, I also propose these three practical steps to help us ensure we take it further.

segments.speaker: Pempo · African Union
segments.text: Let's document the policy recommendations from this session, looking at our colleagues from UNDP who have been very, very supportive and fundamental to the African Youth Charter at 20 campaign. Secondly, let us explore a small set of youth-designated Creatives for Peace pilots within the different member states, as well as all those that were not represented within the Co-Creators Council. And also leveraging on UNDP and creative networks that have already been established.

segments.speaker: Pempo · African Union
segments.text: Each should have a local partner, a budget, safeguards, and clear community objectives and a review date. Third, let us agree how to measure progress. Something very, very important within the space that we live.
